title: The Do Now: Active Ingredients
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane revisits his "Do Now" classroom routine a year after his original post, this time isolating the "active ingredients" that make the routine work rather than describing it from scratch. He starts from an unusual premise: the Do Now is the least useful instructional time in his lesson, since students arrive at different times, supplies go missing, and interruptions pile up, so the routine's job is to be simple and resilient rather than instructionally ambitious. His actual routine is deliberately minimal -- a half-sheet handout, five projected retrieval questions students answer in about three minutes, quick self-checking, and occasional grading to signal that the practice matters. Kane lists the specific features he thinks matter most: low prep time, a strict three-minute cap, retrieval-only content on material already taught, avoiding more than one question likely to be missed, circulating to sample one question closely rather than trying to track all five, and a spaced-practice spreadsheet (inspired by Lee Wheeler) that schedules which skills to retrieve and when. He argues the biggest mistake teachers make is trying to do too much with the Do Now -- previewing new content or building elaborate warm-ups -- when the constrained, chaotic first minutes of class can't reliably support that ambition. The result is a routine explicitly designed to be boring: confidence-building retrieval practice and a small amount of real-time diagnostic data, nothing more.
points: Kane's central claim is that the Do Now is the least useful instructional time in a lesson (arrivals, attendance, interruptions), so the routine should be deliberately simple rather than ambitious -- trying to preview new content in those first few minutes usually backfires.

His "active ingredients" are a strict three-minute cap, low prep time (about one minute to write daily questions), and content limited to retrieval practice on material already taught rather than new or complex problems.
He deliberately avoids putting more than one likely-to-be-missed question on the Do Now, reasoning that more than that both undermines confidence and generates more data than he can usefully act on.

During the three minutes he circulates and closely samples just one question across every student's paper, judging that tracking more than one question in real time is too much data to act on reliably.

A spaced-practice spreadsheet (built on a Fibonacci-interval idea borrowed from Lee Wheeler) automatically schedules which previously taught skills come back for retrieval and when, preventing him from forgetting or over-repeating topics.
quotes: In my opinion, the Do Now is the least useful instructional time in a lesson. I have students coming in at different times. I need to take attendance. Two students don't have pencils.

I think the most common mistake teachers make with a Do Now is trying to do too much. It's tempting to create a warmup activity that previews what students are about to learn, getting right to the heart of the lesson. I think that's often a mistake.
The routine is short. The Do Now is the least useful instructional time in a lesson. I aim for three minutes flat, from the start of class until I go over the questions.

All questions are retrieval practice on topics students have learned previously and are relatively straightforward. There will be time for more complex questions later when I have the chance to provide more scaffolding and support.
I avoid putting more than one question on the Do Now that I'm uncertain students will get right. If half the class is getting two or three or four questions wrong, I screwed up.

When I circulate around the room, I pick the question I think students are most likely to struggle with and look at every student's paper to see their answers. I find I can reliably do this for one question.
The spreadsheet automatically schedules retrieval practice for each skill, beginning with several days of retrieval in a row before spacing out practice at larger and larger intervals.
